newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: FOCUS - Yukong hopeful China refinery will go ahead.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Yukong hopeful China refinery will go ahead.

text.p: South Korea's Yukong Ltd is keeping alive hopes for permission to build a refinery in China, believing it meets more concerns of state planners than a project by Royal Dutch/Shell dropped last week.

Analysts said Yukong's prospects were still unclear after a 16-month wait, but it stood a better chance than Royal/Dutch Shell's joint-venture project which fell by the wayside last week after an even longer eight-year wait.
"It's taking time, but we are hopeful that the project would go ahead," a manager involved in the China project at Yukong said by telephone.
The Yukong plan is to build a 100,000 barrels-per-day export refinery in the thriving special economic zone of Shenzhen, bordering Hong Kong.
The project would include a 40,000-bpd residue fluid catalytic cracker and a 50,000-bpd residue hydro desulpheriser -- refinery units that upgrade the value of products.
Yukong had expected a decision on the refinery by early 1996, but the deadline came and went and analysts said doubts are now rising as to whether China wants foreign refiners at all.

Last week Chinese sources said Royal Dutch/Shell's plans to build a 160,000-bpd refinery with Chinese partners had been dropped from a plan to build a $6 billion refining and petrochemical project because of concerns over too much refinery capacity and profit margins.
Shell said the refinery project was on hold and that it hoped to build a refinery at a later date.

Industry analysts said China wants to limit new refinery investment in the mainland to protect the domestic industry. Its policy is to expand existing refineries rather than construct new ones, they said.
But analysts said Yukong hoped to get a long term foot-on-the-door with its proposal that would eventually allow it access to the domestic market.

Under the proposal, all output from the Shenzhen facility would be for export and the project would be entirely financed offshore -- meeting two of China's major concerns with new refinery projects. Major export markets are seen as Hong Kong and Southeast Asia.

"Prospects for Yukong are not very good," said a U.S. analyst who declined to be named. "But if Yukong sticks to the promise of purely export refinery, 100-percent owned by Yukong with its output sold outside of China, then it has a better chance to be approved."
Analysts said Beijing may be more hesitant about Yukong since the company has little experience in building and operating refineries outside South Korea.
"Yukong, if it really wants it, has to give up a lot, whereas bigger players with better reputation can demand a lot," said Bill Hunsaker, an energy analyst at ING-Barings Securities.
But analysts said giving up the Chinese market initially was not such a good idea.
"It would be a foolish thing to set up a big refinery in China and not be able to sell it there," the U.S. analyst said.
